title: How 911 Finds Your Phone, Even Inside a Building
summary: Follow one 911 call: which center answers, how a landline arrives with an address, how a cell phone is placed on a map from tower to coordinates to height, and why the floor is still the hardest part. Plus text to 911, Canada's T9-1-1 and the move to Next Generation 911.
sources: Consumers make 240 million calls to 911 each year, and in many areas 80% or more are from wireless phones; z-axis (vertical) accuracy of plus or minus 3 meters for 80% of indoor wireless E911 calls, in the top 25 markets by 3 Apr 2021 and the top 50 by 3 Apr 2023; nearly all smartphones appear to have barometric pressure sensors; it is not now technically feasible to reliably convert z-axis data to a floor level and no authoritative floor database exists; dispatchable location = street address, floor level and office or apartment number (FCC Fifth Report and Order, Wireless E911 Location Accuracy Requirements, Federal Register, 16 Jan 2020): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2020-01-16/html/2019-28483.htm

Dispatchable location or x/y location within 50 meters for 40% of wireless 911 calls within 2 years, 50% within 3, 70% within 5 and 80% within 6 years; the majority of wireless calls are now made indoors; satellite-based location does not give accurate location for many wireless calls; test data cited: successful indoor GPS fixes were 23 percent in urban environments (FCC Fourth Report and Order, Wireless E911 Location Accuracy Requirements, Federal Register, 4 Mar 2015): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2015-03-04/html/2015-04424.htm

Phase I: relay the caller's number (ANI) and the location of the cell site or base station receiving the 911 call; Phase II: identify the caller's latitude and longitude within 125 meters in 67 percent of cases, within five years of the 1 Oct 1996 effective date (FCC E911 Report and Order, Federal Register, 2 Aug 1996): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1996-08-02/html/96-19662.htm

Wireless 911 calls have historically been routed by the location of the cell tower that handles the call; ATIS estimates that on average 12% of wireless legacy E911 voice calls are misrouted; location-based routing is required when the caller's location is known within 165 meters at 90% confidence (nationwide carriers within 6 months, rules effective 13 May 2024); device-based hybrid location uses crowd-sourced Wi-Fi, A-GNSS and other handset sensors (FCC Report and Order, Location-Based Routing for Wireless 911 Calls, Federal Register, 13 Mar 2024): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-03-13/html/2024-03157.htm

2021 data: 45 states reported 213,652,929 total 911 calls; 49 states reported 4,637 primary PSAPs; 38 states reported 507,969 texts to 911 (NHTSA National 911 Program, National 911 Annual Report: 2021 Data): https://www.911.gov/assets/2021-911-Profile-Database-Report_FINAL.pdf

The US 911 system is operated by local and state government; where text-to-911 is not available, the sender gets a bounce-back message (911.gov, Frequently asked questions): https://911.gov/calling-911/frequently-asked-questions

NG911 is a digital, internet protocol (IP)-based system that will replace the analog 911 infrastructure; it allows voice, photos, videos and text messages to flow from the public to the 911 network (911.gov, Next Generation 911): https://www.911.gov/issues/ng911

The selective router directs a 911 call to the appropriate PSAP; the PSAP equipment sends the caller's number (ANI) to the 911 database, which performs an ALI (automatic location identification) look-up and returns the caller's location to the call taker (California Governor's Office of Emergency Services, 9-1-1 system description, chapter II): https://www.caloes.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/PSC/Documents/Chapter-II-System-Description.pdf

9-1-1 call centres are operated by municipal and provincial/territorial governments; with Enhanced 9-1-1 the caller's phone number and address are automatically provided; enhanced wireless 9-1-1 uses GPS and/or trilateration (the signal's distance from nearby towers), generally within 50 to 300 meters; text with 9-1-1 for hearing or speech impaired Canadians: registered users dial 9-1-1 and the operator gets a notification to communicate by text (CRTC, 9-1-1 services for traditional wireline, VoIP and wireless phone services): https://crtc.gc.ca/eng/phone/911/can.htm

Revised deadline of 31 March 2027 for the transition to NG9-1-1, an improved service with Internet Protocol (IP)-based capabilities, including text messages based on real-time text (Telecom Decision CRTC 2025-67; kept by Telecom Decision CRTC 2025-291): https://crtc.gc.ca/eng/archive/2025/2025-67.htm

Text with 9-1-1 (T9-1-1) is only for deaf, deafened, hard of hearing or speech impaired persons, who must register with their wireless provider (Text with 9-1-1, history): https://www.textwith911.ca/en/history/
Pressure decreases with height (US National Weather Service, pressure training page): https://www.weather.gov/source/zhu/ZHU_Training_Page/winds/pressure_winds/Pressure.htm

scenes.narration: Every call to {911|nine one one} starts with one question: where are you?
Americans make an estimated {240 million|two hundred forty million} of those calls a year.
Most come from cell phones. So how does {911|nine one one} find a phone that could be anywhere? Even inside a building?
For years, cell calls were routed by the tower they reached. By one industry estimate, about {12%|twelve percent} landed at the wrong {911|nine one one} center.
By the end, you'll know who picks up, how a phone lands on a map, what changed the routing, and why floors are the hardest part.
Part one: who picks up.
Follow one call. It rings at a public safety answering point, run by local or state government.
In {2021|twenty twenty-one}, {49|forty-nine} states reported {4,637|four thousand six hundred thirty-seven} primary centers.
On a landline, the system already knows where you are.
A router reads the number and picks the right center. A database lookup then puts the address on the call taker's screen.
Canada's enhanced {9-1-1|nine one one} works the same way: number and address arrive automatically.
Like seeing what runs behind the walls? Subscribe. There's a new system every Sunday.
Part two: the phone.
A cell phone has no address on file. So the system narrows in, step by step.
Step one, in the FCC's first rules from {1996|nineteen ninety-six}: the location of the cell site that took the call.
Step two: latitude and longitude, within {125|a hundred twenty-five} meters in {67%|sixty-seven percent} of calls, by {2001|two thousand one}.
The catch: most cell calls are now made indoors, where satellite signals can struggle.
In one test the FCC cited, GPS got an indoor fix just {23%|twenty-three percent} of the time in cities.
So in {2015|twenty fifteen}, the FCC raised the bar: within {50|fifty} meters for {80%|eighty percent} of wireless calls, within six years.
Today, the phone itself helps. Device-based location blends satellite signals, nearby Wi-Fi, and the phone's own sensors.
And those wrong turns? In {2024|twenty twenty-four}, the FCC told carriers to route by the phone's location, not the tower, when it's known within {165|a hundred sixty-five} meters.
Canada's carriers use GPS, or measure the distance to nearby towers: generally within {50|fifty} to {300|three hundred} meters.
Part three: the floor.
A dot on a map can land on the right building and still miss the floor.
So the FCC added height: within {3|three} meters for {80%|eighty percent} of indoor calls, biggest markets first.
How? Nearly all smartphones carry a pressure sensor, and air pressure drops as you go up.
But a height isn't a floor. In {2019|twenty nineteen}, the FCC found no database that could reliably convert one to the other.
That's why the rules also accept a dispatchable location: street address, floor and apartment.
Some calls aren't calls. In {2021|twenty twenty-one}, {38|thirty-eight} states reported {507,969|over half a million} texts to {911|nine one one}.
In Canada, texting {9-1-1|nine one one} is for people who are deaf, hard of hearing or speech impaired. They register, then the call continues by text.
And {911|nine one one} is moving onto internet technology. Next Generation {911|nine one one} can carry photos, video and texts.
Canada's deadline to switch: March {31|thirty-first}, {2027|twenty twenty-seven}.
So, where are you? A landline answers with an address. A phone, with a tower, a dot, then a height. The floor is still the hardest step.
Pick a hatch for the next system. A new one every Sunday.
